catalog_quote: Word stress is free in Ukrainian (Brovčenko 1969). It can be contrastive: ˈkury [ˈkurɪ] 'chicken' (pl) vs. kuˈry [kuˈrɪ] 'to smoke' or doˈroha [dɔˈrɔɦa] 'road' vs. doroˈha [dɔrɔˈɦa] 'dear'. The main stress can appear on any syllable in a given word, e.g. ˈvy-ra-xu-va-nyj [ˈʋɪraxuʋanɪj] 'calculated', za-ˈlja-ku-va-ty [zaˈlʲakuʋatɪ] 'to intimidate', po-vi-ˈdo-my-ty [pɔʋʲiˈdɔmɪtɪ] 'to inform', pry-sto-su-ˈva-nec' [prɪstɔsuˈʋanɛtsʲ] 'conformist', pe-re-po-vi-ˈsty [pɛrɛpɔʋʲiˈstɪ] 'to relate' (Danylenko & Vakulenko 1995: 13). The stress can also move within a paradigm: ro-ˈby-ty [rɔˈbɪtɪ] 'to do', ro-ˈblju [rɔˈblʲu] 'I do', ˈro-byš [ˈrɔbɪʃ] 'you do' (de Bray 1951: 74). It is sensitive to morphology and its shifting nature reinforces the distinctive function of morphological constituents; for a historical background of the 'morphologization' of stress see Shevelov (1979: 120–126). sweep_summary: Two title hits for Ukrainian (ukra1253, catalog kind 'lexical', deciding source Pompino-Marschall et al. 2017 JIPA). (1) Yanovich & Steriade 2010 is an unpublished OCP talk with no open text found; its published successor, Steriade & Yanovich 2015 'Accentual allomorphs in East Slavic' (Equinox, 60-page chapter), is open on Steriade's MIT page and was fetched sources and read: stress position in Ukrainian is 'in principle unconstrained' with four lexical accentual noun classes, plus a preference for penultimate stress in standard Ukrainian (invariant penult reported for some Western dialects) — confirms and refines the catalog's lexical coding; does not supersede the JIPA illustration as deciding source. (2) Al'muhamedova & Kul'sharipova 1980 is about Russian o-kanje dialects; Glottolog's Ukrainian link is a flagged computerized misassignment from 'slova' — irrelevant, priority none. Saved: (+.txt), and updated. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, archive.org and Google were rate-limited, so discovery relied on Glottolog, Crossref, DuckDuckGo/Bing (empty), lingbuzz and author pages.

new_statements.quote: The East Slavic accentual systems have a shared characteristic: the position of the stress is in principle unconstrained. In Ukrainian, however, penultimate stress is preferred. In some Western Ukrainian dialects, this preference is reported as an invariant fact (Zilynskyj 1979: 184, 194; Reiter 1969; Baerman 1999). The data we analyse – from standard Ukrainian, based on Eastern dialect – show that aspects of the penult preference are present in general.

new_statements.reading: Ukrainian word stress is lexically determined (position 'in principle unconstrained'; nouns belong to four lexically indexed accentual classes with fixed-stem, post-accenting and mobile patterns), overlaid with a statistical/markedness preference for penultimate main stress in standard (Eastern) Ukrainian and a reported fixed-penult pattern in some Western dialects. This confirms the catalog's 'lexical' coding and refines it by naming the penult bias (450 penult vs 370 final vs 55 antepenult among database base nouns).
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (60 pp., text layer present; PDF p. 10 = book p. 263, section 7.2.1 'Preference for penult stress in modern Ukrainian': the reported quotation matches the extracted text output word for word, including the parenthetical '(Zilynskyj 1979: 184, 194; Reiter 1969; Baerman 1999)'. The passage continues: 'Having relied on secondary literature and dictionary data for the evidence of penult-stress preference, we do not know its exact extent across Ukrainian vernaculars' (p. 263) - i.e. the penult-preference evidence is explicitly second-hand (Zilynskyj's self-transcriptions, dictionaries), which is why it cannot supersede a first-hand phonetic description. new_statements.second_reader_bearing_note: Agree: 'lexical' stands. Refinement only: record the penult-markedness bias as a statistical tendency in standard (Eastern) Ukrainian, and the fixed-penult report for some Western dialects (Zilynskyj 1979: 184, 194; Reiter 1969; Baerman 1999) as a dialect note. Do not cite the 450/370/55 base-noun counts as a lexicon-wide frequency: the database (sec. 7.2.5, pp. 269-270) was seeded from Butska's (2002) core set of mobile nouns and, by the authors' own admission, under-records penult-stressed faithful derivatives; the lexicon-scale statistic is table (9), p. 265 (ISUM, N=3385 -ov-yj adjectives…

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim in the held JIPA 2017 text layer at the stated section, and the De Bray 1969 p.74 backup line is in the held archive.org text. The deciding source is a 2017 JIPA Illustration by phoneticians citing the Ukrainian experimental monograph (Brovčenko 1969); the classification 'lexical' (free, contrastive, paradigmatically mobile, weight-insensitive, no positional default) is uncontroversial and is restated word-for-word in the two open instrumental papers fetched sources now (Mołczanow et al. 2018 SP p.908: 'Ukrainian has lexical primary stress... can appear in any syllable'; Łukaszewicz & Mołczanow 2024 SP p.285: 'weight-insensitive lexical stress... any syllable'). sources.quote: 'Ukrainian has weight-insensitive lexical stress, which is expressed phonetically by prolonged vowel duration ([1]-[5]). Lexical stress can appear in any syllable of the word, as illustrated by the minimal pairs in (1)' [ˈsɛstrɨ]/[sɛˈstrɨ], [dɔˈrɔɦa]/[ˌdɔrɔˈɦa]; increased duration in unstressed word-initial/medial/final positions 'has been interpreted to manifest rhythmic (grammatical) stress'; acoustic results (14 speakers) 'corroborate the existence of word-final rhythmic stress in Ukrainian' independent of boundary lengthening.

sources.citation: Mołczanow, Janina, Beata Łukaszewicz & Anna Łukaszewicz. 2018. Rhythmic stress or word-boundary effects? Comparison of primary and secondary stress correlates in segmentally identical word pairs. Proceedings of Speech Prosody 2018 (Poznań), 908-912. doi:10.21437/SpeechProsody.2018-183.
sources.quote: 'Ukrainian has lexical primary stress and predictable rhythmic stress. Lexical stress can appear in any syllable of the word ... The most salient cue to primary stress is duration.' Traditional sources report subsidiary stress; 'rhythmic stresses are placed at both word edges, with additional rhythmic beats intervening between the primary and the secondary stresses, e.g. velosypedýst [ˌʋɛlɔˌsɨpɛˈdɨst]'. Pilot acoustic study (4 speakers, segmentally identical pairs popádaty/popadáty) finds duration differences depending on presence vs absence of (rhythmic) stress.

sources.quote: Abstract: acoustic study of secondary stress in polysyllabic words with lexical stress at/near the right edge; 'Ukrainian has an iteration of secondary stresses from the left edge towards the lexical stress', making it a bidirectional system with internal lapses (like Polish).
sources.note: The full instrumental account of Ukrainian secondary stress (left-edge iteration toward the lexical stress plus edge prominence); our srule currently says 'no agreed pattern' after Zilyns'kyj 1979 apud Pompino-Marschall — this is the source to re-read the secondary-stress note against.

sources.quote: The East Slavic accentual systems have a shared characteristic: the position of the stress is in principle unconstrained. In Ukrainian, however, penultimate stress is preferred. In some Western Ukrainian dialects, this preference is reported as an invariant fact (Zilynskyj 1979: 184, 194; Reiter 1969; Baerman 1999). The data we analyse – from standard Ukrainian, based on Eastern dialect – show that aspects of the penult preference are present in general. [...] Ukrainian nouns fall into four main accentual classes, similar to Russian. These differ in the number of accentual allomorphs found in inflection: class (a) nouns have one stem allomorph, which is always accented; classes (b)–(d) have typically more than one, almost always including an unstressed allomorph.
